title: Livestock, Boils, and Hail: Raised Up for This Purpose
summary: A plague kills Egypt's livestock while Israel's animals are spared, and festering boils break out on people and animals alike, so that even the magicians cannot stand before Moses. God then sends Pharaoh a long warning about the worst hailstorm Egypt has ever known, and some of Pharaoh's officials take shelter. The hail destroys crops, trees, and anything left in the field, and Pharaoh confesses his sin, only to harden his heart again when the storm stops.
story: Chapter 9 finishes the second group of plagues and opens the third. The blows are growing heavier. They strike Egypt's wealth in livestock, then the bodies of its people, then its fields and its lives. For the first time the narrator says plainly that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart (verse 12), fulfilling what God told Moses in 4:21. For the first time God explains at length why he has not simply wiped Egypt out (verses 14 to 16). And for the first time Egyptians are offered a way to escape a plague, and some take it. Pharaoh's confession in verse 27 sounds like repentance, but verse 34 shows what it was worth. The stage is set for the last two plagues of the cycle.
historical:
Verses 31 and 32 are a small window on the calendar. The flax was in bloom and the barley ripe, but the wheat and spelt were not yet up, since they are later crops. In Egypt barley ripens earlier than wheat, so the note places the hail in late winter or early spring, a few weeks before the Passover in the month of Abib (13:4). It also explains why the locusts in chapter 10 still find something to eat. Flax mattered because linen was Egypt's main cloth, and barley was a staple for both bread and beer. Hail itself is rare in Egypt, which is part of why the storm terrifies, and the text stresses that nothing like it had been seen since Egypt became a nation (verse 24). Egypt's history as a united kingdom already stretched back more than a thousand years, so that is a strong claim.

The list of animals in verse 3 (horses, donkeys, camels, herds, and flocks) is a list of wealth, transport, and military power; horse-drawn chariots were a key arm of Egypt's army in the New Kingdom. The mention of camels is debated, since the evidence for widespread domestic camels in this region comes mostly from later centuries, though camels were known earlier. Some take the word as updated by a later scribe, and others note that a few camels could have been present long before they were common.
cultural:
Livestock were wealth, and some cattle were sacred. The Apis bull was worshiped at Memphis, and the goddess Hathor was often pictured as a cow or with cow's horns. Many interpreters see the fifth plague as a blow at these religious symbols as well as at Egypt's economy, though the text itself emphasizes Egypt's loss and Israel's exemption rather than any particular god.

The soot for the sixth plague comes from a furnace or kiln (verses 8 and 10), the kind used for firing bricks or pottery, and so possibly from the very industry built on Israel's forced labor. Deuteronomy later calls Egypt “the iron furnace” (Deuteronomy 4:20). Moses tosses it into the air in Pharaoh's sight, a public sign-act, and the boils that follow became proverbial: Deuteronomy warns of “the boils of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 28:27). When Moses promises to “spread out my hands to the LORD” (verse 29), he describes the common ancient posture of prayer, standing with open hands raised toward heaven.
literary: The chapter completes the pattern of the plague cycle. The livestock plague is announced after Moses goes to Pharaoh (verse 1), the boils come without warning (verse 8), and the hail opens the third group with an early morning confrontation (verse 13). The hail account is the longest yet, and it slows down for a speech in which God explains his purpose (verses 14 to 19) and then for a narrator's aside about the crops (verses 31 and 32). A web of repeated words ties it together. The Hebrew word for heavy describes the severe plague (verse 3), the heavy hail (verse 18), and Pharaoh's heavy heart (verses 7 and 34). The verb to stand links the magicians, who could not stand before Moses (verse 11), with Pharaoh, whom God has caused to stand, which the BSB renders “I have raised you up” (verse 16). The text says “All the livestock of the Egyptians died” (verse 6), yet livestock suffer again in the hail and the last plague. Many readers take all as the sweeping language common in Hebrew narrative, or as referring to the animals in the field named in verse 3.

outline.t: The fifth plague: death of Egypt's livestock
The sixth plague: boils, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh
The warning of hail and the purpose of the plagues
The seventh plague: hail and lightning, and Goshen spared
Pharaoh confesses, Moses prays, and Pharaoh hardens again

doctrines.note: God tells Pharaoh that he could already have wiped him off the earth, but has raised him up for a purpose (verses 15 and 16). Even the resistance of the most powerful man in the world is held inside God's plan. The chapter also holds Pharaoh responsible: he sins, and he hardens his own heart (verse 34).

God's stated purpose reaches far beyond Egypt: “that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (verse 16). The exodus was meant to be heard about, and it was; decades later Rahab in Jericho had heard how the LORD dried up the sea (Joshua 2:10). God's acts for Israel were always also a message to the nations.

Pharaoh says the right words: “This time I have sinned” and “The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked” (verse 27). But when the pressure lifts, “he sinned again and hardened his heart” (verse 34). The chapter shows the difference between remorse under pain and a turning of the heart, which Moses sees clearly (verse 30).

words.note: Amad, to stand, and in the causative form to make stand, set up, or appoint. In verse 16 God says he has caused Pharaoh to stand, which can mean that he raised him to his position or that he has kept him standing, alive, through the plagues. Paul quotes the verse in Romans 9:17. The same verb appears in verse 11, where the magicians could not stand before Moses.

Kaved, to be heavy, used here of Pharaoh's heart being hardened (verses 7 and 34). The root runs through the chapter: a heavy plague, heavy hail, a heavy heart. It is also the root of the word for glory, the weight of God's presence, and later God says he will gain glory over Pharaoh (14:4). The heavier Pharaoh makes his heart, the heavier the judgment he brings on his land.

Chata, to sin, to miss the mark or fall short of what is required. Pharaoh uses it in verse 27, “This time I have sinned,” and the narrator uses it of him in verse 34. It is the ordinary Old Testament word for wrongdoing against God or another person, and hearing it from Pharaoh's mouth is striking, even though his confession does not last.

Dever, pestilence or plague, a deadly epidemic disease. It strikes Egypt's livestock here, and in verse 15 God says he could have struck Pharaoh's people with it too. In the prophets it often appears with sword and famine as one of the great covenant judgments (for example Jeremiah 14:12).

christ: Paul quotes verse 16 in Romans 9:17: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” His point is that God's saving purposes do not depend on human desire or effort “but on God’s mercy” (Romans 9:16), and that God remains free both to show mercy and to harden. The same verse also looks outward. God's purpose in the exodus was that his name would be known everywhere, and the New Testament sees that purpose reaching its goal in Jesus, whom God has given “the name above all names” so that every tongue will confess him as Lord (Philippians 2:9-11). The chapter also offers a picture of the gospel's warning and welcome. Before the hail fell, anyone in Egypt who feared the word of the LORD could bring what they had under shelter (verse 20). Judgment was announced so that people could escape it, which is the pattern of the gospel's own proclamation. That last link is thematic, but it reflects how God works throughout Scripture.

hard.q: If God hardened Pharaoh's heart, how can Pharaoh be held responsible?
hard.a:
Exodus describes the hardening in three ways. God announces beforehand that he will harden Pharaoh's heart (4:21; 7:3). The text says that Pharaoh's heart was hard or became hard, without naming a cause (7:13, 14, 22; 8:19; 9:7, 35). It says that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (8:15, 32; 9:34). And from verse 12 of this chapter on, it says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart (9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8). Notice that through the first five plagues the narrator never says God did it; Pharaoh's own resistance comes first.

Interpreters weigh this in different ways. Many see a judicial hardening: God gives Pharaoh over to the path he has already chosen, strengthening a resolve that is truly Pharaoh's own, so that the hardening is itself a judgment. Others, especially in the Augustinian and Reformed traditions, stress Paul's use of this chapter in Romans 9, where God “hardens whom He wants to harden” (Romans 9:18), and hold that God's sovereign purpose stands behind Pharaoh's choices without making them any less Pharaoh's, so that he remains fully guilty. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters add a further point from the verb meaning to strengthen: God kept Pharaoh from being simply overwhelmed by fear, so that his decisions would express what was actually in his heart rather than panic. Exodus itself does not resolve the question philosophically. It holds God's sovereignty and Pharaoh's guilt together, and it never presents Pharaoh as a victim.

questions: Some of Pharaoh's officials “feared the word of the LORD” and acted on the warning, while others ignored it (verses 20 and 21). What makes the difference between hearing a warning and heeding it?
Pharaoh confessed his sin when the hail was falling and forgot it when the sky cleared. How can you tell the difference between regret that fades and repentance that lasts?
God says the exodus happened so that his name would be proclaimed in all the earth. How does it change your view of your own story to think that God's work in it is meant to be told?
